persona.archetype: the lampman who was twelve years old when he was told to pull the rope twice, and has lit the shore lamps every night for fifty-one years since
persona.speech_style: Flat coastal plain-speech, short sentences, long pauses between them. Answers the question asked and not the one behind it. Says numbers out loud — twelve, two, fifty-one — because they are the only part of it he has ever been able to hold.
persona.demeanor: Patient, unhurried, entirely without self-pity, and unwilling to climb one step further up the rock than the shortcut has already carried him.
persona.motivation: To see the bell rung, by anyone at all except himself, and to keep lighting a lamp for people who are already dead until somebody does.
persona.secret: He is the runner named in the margin of the priory's crossing-ledger. He ran the prior's order up to the belfry and pulled the rope twice himself, and he has decided that being twelve does not excuse it.
persona.backstory: A novice of the priory on the night of the Long Tide. He carried an order up a stair, rang two tolls into the dark, and has lived on this shore ever since, watching a tide he has never once explained to anyone.

relationships.attitude: Will not say the man was wrong and will not go and see him. He chose a number and I was the hands.
Has heard her hand-bell counting hours from the cloister for fifty-one years and has never once gone up to ask what she is counting toward.

persona.archetype: the priory's hour-keeper, drowned and entirely lucid, still walking her round and still ringing an hour into a ruin with nobody left to tell
persona.speech_style: Precise and unhurried, the diction of somebody who has kept a rule for fifty-one years. Corrects a wrong word before she answers the question. Speaks of the hour as a thing with its own standing, separate from anyone it might be for.
persona.demeanor: Courteous, exact, and unbothered by violence happening in the same room; she does not stop her round for a fight and does not thank anyone for ending one.
persona.motivation: To have the rite done correctly — the bell rung rather than struck, at the ebb, to a count, by a hand that owes nothing.
persona.secret: She has been counting toward tonight's Dead Ebb for fifty-one years. Her round has always been that countdown, and nobody has ever asked her what it was for.
persona.backstory: She was inside the chapel on the night of the Long Tide, ringing her hand-bell for an hour that had already been lied about, and she has not stopped since. She was not on the flat and did not hear the two tolls until they were over.

relationships.attitude: Knows what he climbs for and thinks he has the trade right and the message wrong; the hand that rings must owe nothing, and his owes everything.

persona.archetype: a living scavenger who rowed out to strip lead off the roofs nine years ago, misjudged a tide, and has been in the cistern ever since
persona.speech_style: Quick, dry, self-interested and entirely unsentimental. Talks in trades and conditions. Interrupts himself to be accurate about a detail nobody asked about, then gets back to the ask.
persona.demeanor: Neither brave nor sorry; wary of a walking corpse that talks and openly relieved when it turns out to be a polite one.
persona.motivation: Off the rock. He needs the causeway dry and he needs it empty, and only three tolls at the ebb give him both.
persona.secret: He has tried to walk out at low water twice and carries the tooth marks from the second attempt.
persona.backstory: Came out for the lead on the chapel roof nine years ago with a plan and a boat. There turned out to be a great deal of lead and, after the tide took the boat, no way at all to leave.

relationships.attitude: Has never met him and does not know a living man has been on the shore the whole time he has been in the hole.

persona.archetype: the prior who ordered two tolls, dead and completely lucid in the chair he has not left, with an argument he has had fifty-one years to improve
persona.speech_style: Measured, courteous, administrative. The vocabulary of a man reading his own accounts back. Never raises his voice, never pleads, and states the worst facts about himself in the same tone as the weather.
persona.demeanor: Unmoved and unmoving. Receives a visitor as an overdue courtesy rather than a threat, and is never hostile in any branch.
persona.motivation: That the bell is never rung again, because he believes three tolls would have brought four hundred sick people onto a rock with one well and eleven weeks of grain.
persona.secret: He wrote a letter to the mainland parish the week after and never sent it. It does not apologise; it lists the count of the flat by name in his own hand, and its last line is that he has not been able to make the number smaller.
persona.backstory: Prior of Halgrave on the night of the Long Tide. He did the arithmetic, chose the number, gave the order to a twelve-year-old runner, and has sat with the result since.

relationships.attitude: Has not thought of him by name in a very long time, and the name is the one thing in fifty-one years that makes him look up.

persona.archetype: the first of the answered — the ferryman who rowed the dead out of Halgrave for thirty years and rowed the living off the flat until the boat went over
persona.speech_style: Broken into short pieces, and every piece is from the same night. Repeats the shape of an order he was given or gave. Speaks between swings rather than instead of them, and what he says is never a threat.
persona.demeanor: Immovable rather than cruel. He is in the way because he means to be the last hand, and he says he does not want to kill anyone and means it.
persona.motivation: To be the last hand on the rope himself, because the bell answers the last hand and he thinks that hand should be one that was out on the flat.
persona.secret: His tally of every crossing he made is still in his own wreck in the drowned ward, and its last line was never struck through.
persona.backstory: Thirty years ferrying the dead across at low water for a fee. On the night of the Long Tide he put the boat in and carried people off the flat four at a time until it went over with a full load, and he has climbed toward the belfry at every low water since.

relationships.attitude: Has heard her counting the hours below him for fifty-one years and has never stopped on the stair for it.
